sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The cold desert of Mongolia and northern China.
why: It separated the Mongolian steppe from China; the Great Wall and the Hexi Corridor run along its southern edge.

name: Sahara

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The largest hot desert, across North Africa.
why: It split Africa into a Mediterranean world and a sub-Saharan one until camels (from about 300 CE) made the gold and salt caravans possible.

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)
Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

name: Persian Gulf

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

why: From Dilmun to Hormuz to oil tankers it has linked Mesopotamia to India and the world.

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

name: Alps

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The great arc of mountains across south-central Europe.
why: Hannibal crossed it to invade Italy, and for 2,000 years the passes (Brenner, Great St Bernard) decided how Germany and Italy connected.

name: Andes

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The longest continental range, along western South America.
why: The Inca ran the largest empire of the Americas along its spine with road networks and terraced valleys.

name: Caucasus Mountains

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The range between the Black and Caspian seas.
why: It was the classic barrier against steppe nomads; only the Darial Gorge and the Derbent coast road crossed it, both fortified since antiquity.

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

name: Himalayas

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The world's highest range, along the northern edge of the Indian subcontinent.
why: It sealed India off from China for most of history, so the two civilisations met mainly by sea or through Central Asia, and its snowmelt feeds the Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra.

name: Hindu Kush

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The high range across Afghanistan, westward continuation of the Pamirs.
why: Every invasion of India from the northwest, from Alexander to Babur, had to cross it, usually by the Khyber; its name is often read as 'killer of Hindus' for the slaves who died crossing.

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

name: Tian Shan

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The 'Heavenly Mountains' of Central Asia, between Kazakhstan and the Tarim Basin.
why: The Silk Road split to run along its north and south feet, and the Dzungarian Gate at its east end was the nomads' highway into the west.

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

name: Ural Mountains

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: Low, old mountains running north-south through Russia.
why: The conventional line between Europe and Asia, though so low that nomads and Russian traders crossed it easily; Russia's conquest of Siberia started just beyond.

name: Zagros Mountains

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The long wall of folded ridges between the Mesopotamian plain and the Iranian plateau.
why: For 5,000 years it was the frontier between lowland empires (Sumer, Babylon, Rome, the Ottomans) and highland ones (Elam, Persia), crossed at a few gaps like the Persian Gates.

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The vast dry grassland of Kazakhstan.
why: The middle of the Eurasian steppe corridor that let horse nomads move from Mongolia to Hungary.

name: North China Plain

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The flat loess-filled plain of the lower Yellow River.
why: China's original heartland and grain base, and the river's flooding over it has killed millions.

name: North European Plain

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

why: Few natural barriers: armies from Napoleon to Hitler crossed it, which is why Poland's borders kept moving.

name: Pontic-Caspian steppe

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The grassland from the Danube to the Urals north of the Black Sea.
why: The western end of the steppe highway: Indo-Europeans, Scythians, Huns, Khazars, Cumans and the Golden Horde all rode out of it.

name: Sahel

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The semi-arid belt along the Sahara's southern edge.
why: Ghana, Mali and Songhai rose along it, where caravans from the desert met the farmers and gold of the south.

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)
Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

name: Tibetan Plateau

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The highest and largest plateau on Earth, averaging over 4,500 m.
why: It is Asia's water tower (the Yellow, Yangtze, Mekong, Indus and Brahmaputra start here), and it let a thin, high kingdom rival Tang China in the 600s to 800s.

name: Nile

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The river through northeast Africa, longest in the world.
why: Its yearly flood made Egypt possible; a narrow green strip in desert fed one of history's longest-lived states.

name: Yangtze

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: China's longest river, across the middle of the country.
why: The rice-rich lower Yangtze became China's economic centre after about 1000 CE, and the river was the north-south line of many divided eras.

name: Arabian Sea

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The northwest Indian Ocean between Arabia and India.
why: Monsoon winds that reverse each season let ships cross it directly, the engine of Indian Ocean trade since Roman times.

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

name: Black Sea

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The inland sea north of Anatolia.
why: Its grain fed Athens and Constantinople, and it connects the steppe rivers to the Mediterranean through the Bosporus.

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

name: Caspian Sea

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The largest lake on Earth, below sea level.
why: A closed sea that steered steppe traffic around its north (the Volga) and south (the Derbent and Caspian gates).

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)
Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

name: Mediterranean Sea

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The almost-enclosed sea between Europe, Africa and Asia.
why: Calm, tideless and ringed with harbours, it let Phoenicians, Greeks, Romans and Venetians knit three continents together.

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

name: Red Sea

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

why: The sea lane from India to Egypt and the Mediterranean, opened by monsoon sailing and later by the Suez Canal.

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

why: It funnelled invaders from the northwest towards the Punjab and Delhi rather than straight into the Gangetic heartland.

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

why: The Silk Road had to cross it between the Tarim Basin and Bactria, and in the 1800s it was where the British and Russian empires nearly touched in the Great Game.

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

why: It splits China into the dry wheat north and the wet rice south, and protected the Wei valley capitals Xi'an and Chang'an.

why: It walled Anatolia off from Syria; armies from Alexander to the Crusaders squeezed through the Cilician Gates, and it was the Byzantine-Arab frontier for 300 years.

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

why: The homeland of the Xiongnu, the Turks and the Mongols, whose horses could only be raised on grass like this.

why: The land bridge between Europe and Asia: Hittites, Persians, Romans, Byzantines, Seljuks and Ottomans all built empires on it.

name: Amu Darya

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

why: The ancient line between Iran and Turan; Bactria and Khwarazm flourished along it.

why: The Roman frontier for 400 years and the road into Europe for nomads and Ottomans alike.

name: Euphrates

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The western river of Mesopotamia.
why: Ur, Babylon and Mari stood on it, and it was the Roman-Persian frontier for 600 years.

name: Ganges

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The holy river of northern India.
why: The heartland of Magadha, the Buddha and the Mauryas, and still India's densest farmland.

name: Indus

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The great river of Pakistan.
why: The Harappan civilisation grew along it; it gave India its name, and was Alexander's eastern limit.

name: Mekong

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The river from Tibet to the South China Sea.
why: Angkor's rice and fish came from its flood pulse via the Tonle Sap.

name: Niger

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: West Africa's great river, looping through the Sahel.
why: Timbuktu, Gao and Djenne grew on its bend, where desert caravans met river boats.

name: Rhine

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The river from the Alps to the North Sea.
why: The Roman frontier with Germania and later the long contested line between France and Germany; Europe's busiest river trade route.

name: Tigris

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The eastern river of Mesopotamia.
why: Nineveh, Ctesiphon and Baghdad all stood on it.

name: Volga

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: Europe's longest river, flowing to the Caspian.
why: The Viking-Khazar fur and silver route, the seat of the Golden Horde (Sarai), and Russia's spine.

name: Yellow River

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: China's northern great river, named for its silt.
why: The cradle of Chinese civilisation and 'China's Sorrow': its course shifts have killed millions and toppled dynasties.

name: Aegean Sea

sources.cite: Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m physical vectors, v5.1.2 (public domain)

what: The island-scattered sea between Greece and Anatolia.
why: Islands in sight of each other made it the school of Greek seafaring and the stage for Troy, Salamis and the Delian League.
